title: Big Shop — health
description:
The dashboard you open when something looks wrong. Triage first: what is broken, what failed, what is slow - in that order.

Counts rather than rates throughout, because Big Shop has very few users and a percentage over a handful of requests is noise. See `specs/observability.md`.

links.title: Browser errors and web vitals (Frontend Observability)

panels.title: API 5xx
panels.description:
Server errors from the Go API. Any number above zero is worth opening the traces below.

_Counted with `last_over_time`, not `increase()`. At this traffic a status often has a single sample in the window, and `increase()` silently **drops** single-sample series while extrapolating the rest - measured here turning one 400 into five and one 500 into nothing at all. A health panel that answers "0 errors" when the answer is 1 is worse than no panel. The cost is that this is a running total rather than a windowed one; with 14-day retention that is close enough, and the graphs below show when it moved._

panels.description:

panels.title: Failed imports
panels.description:
Imports that ended in `error` - this app or OpenAI failing. Excludes `empty` (the page had nothing on it) and `rejected` (the upload was refused), neither of which is a fault. Both are broken out on the functions dashboard.

panels.title: Requests
panels.description:
Both backend runtimes. Not a health signal - it is here so a zero above can be read correctly. Zero errors out of zero requests means nobody used the app.

_Counted with `last_over_time`, not `increase()`. At this traffic a status often has a single sample in the window, and `increase()` silently **drops** single-sample series while extrapolating the rest - measured here turning one 400 into five and one 500 into nothing at all. A health panel that answers "0 errors" when the answer is 1 is worse than no panel. panels.title: Traces that ended in an error
panels.description:
**Start here, not with the logs.** A failed request records its cause on the span, not in a log line - ADR-0008 section 3 removed service-layer logging precisely so there is one place to look. Open a trace and the exception events carry the wrapped cause.

A Dave turn spans both runtimes and every tool call, so a failure is attributed to the hop that caused it.

panels.title: Error log lines (expected to be sparse)
panels.description:
Nearly always empty, **by design**. The service layer does not log (ADR-0008 section 3); what reaches here is the handful of lines that say a *deployment* is misconfigured - an unset `API_HOST_INTERNAL`, an unreachable catalog lookup - which are facts about the environment rather than about a request.

Each line carries a `trace_id`; click it to open the trace.

_Filtered with `| severity_text="ERROR"` rather than a stream selector: OTLP severity arrives as structured metadata, not as an indexed label, so `{severity_text="ERROR"}` matches nothing at all._

panels.title: Slowest routes, p95
panels.description:
Both runtimes on one axis - possible only because the Netlify histogram was given the same `http_route` and status labels as the Go API's otelhttp one.

The function routes will always sit far above the API routes: they are dominated by an OpenAI call measured in seconds. That is expected, and it is why ADR-0007 is relaxed about the 250ms flush on that side.

panels.title: Requests and database operations
panels.description:
Server spans against database query spans. **The ratio is the point.**

Phase 3 found `GET /shopping-list` issuing around 30 database operations in a single request - an N+1 that was invisible because nothing counted queries. If these two lines diverge, a route has grown a loop.

_Pinned to a 3-hour window with a panel-level time override, independent of the dashboard's range. Tempo rejects TraceQL metrics queries over long ranges - measured here failing at 24h and succeeding at 6h - so without this the panel errors on every load of a dashboard that defaults to 24 hours._

_Grouped with `by (name)` rather than plain `rate()`. TraceQL metrics frames are all named `rate`, and neither `legendFormat` nor a `byFrameRefID` override renames them - both were tried - so two ungrouped queries produce a legend reading "rate, rate". Grouping by span name makes each series label itself, and shows *which* routes and *which* database operations rather than two flat totals._
